Thanks again for the call this morning, Alex — really helpful to walk through FinCo's end-to-end flow. Below is a short recap + concrete next steps so we're aligned.

Recap (what we heard)
- Primary requirement: model answers served with a latency SLO at the 95th percentile. Ballpark target you gave on the call: 100–150ms.
- Context window: you indicated inputs can be long (up to ~8k tokens) for document-aware prompts; some calls will be much shorter (~512 tokens).
- Output size: typical output ~128–256 tokens, occasional bursts up to 512 tokens.
- Concurrency/throughput: sustained QPS estimated ~120 req/s, peak concurrency ~300–400.
- Streaming: preferred for a better UX (progressive scoring), but acceptable to have partial streaming + final completion.

Open technical questions
1) Confirm whether the 95p latency target is for time-to-first-byte (TTFB) or full completion for the full output.
2) Can you share representative prompt sizes (tokens) or a few sample payloads?
3) Are you open to using a model variant with a smaller context window for the majority of traffic and an 8k-capacity variant for rare long requests?

What we'll deliver next
- Performance matrix with expected 95p latencies across common context/output size combos and streaming vs non-streaming (attached).
- Proposed SLA parameters and a pilot runbook (attached: redwood-sla-params.pdf).
- Suggested configuration: streaming + prefix/KV caching for document flows, client-side retry/backoff guidance, autoscaling profile for sustaining ~150 req/s, and quantization profile suggestions for cost/latency tradeoffs.

Next steps
- Alex: share 2–3 representative prompt payloads and confirm whether 95p should be TTFB or end-of-response.
- FinCo: preferred window for pilot kickoff next week?
- Redwood: we will run synthetic perf tests against your sample payloads and share numbers + a recommended initial config within 48 hours.

Thanks — talk soon.
—

Thanks Marissa — great summary. A few clarifications from our side:

- Latency SLO: we care most about time-to-first-byte for interactive UIs (so users see the start quickly) but end-to-response 95p is also important for completeness checks. If pushed, prioritize TTFB <= 120ms at 95p for the 75% of requests that are under 512 tokens; for the long 8k context cases we can relax to ~250ms TTFB but would like final completion within 500–800ms if possible.
- Throughput/concurrency: average sustained is ~120 req/s; expected peak concurrency around 350–400 during batch processing windows.
- Streaming: yes — streaming is an intended part of the product UX for our analysts. We need the first partial tokens quickly (TTFB) and the rest streamed as generated.
- Context windows: we do have a mixed traffic pattern. Roughly 75% of traffic is short (<=512 tokens input), 20% mid (~2k–4k), 5% long (~6k–8k).

I'll attach a couple of sample payloads (anonymized) showing token distributions. Also: what quantization/variant tradeoffs do you recommend for keeping TTFB low on long-context requests?

Timeline: we'd like a pilot next week if you can commit to baseline perf numbers ahead of kickoff.

Alex
Product Lead, FinCo
alex.johnson@finco.com
(attach: sample-payloads.json)

Hi Alex — quick technical notes based on the traffic mix you gave and our internal profiling:

1) Time-to-first-byte vs end-to-response
- Streaming is the most effective lever for TTFB. For short inputs (~512 tokens) we typically see TTFB in the 40–90ms range on an optimized instance (NVSwitch interconnects, latest kernels) and 95p can be ~120ms depending on batching and model size.
- For long-context (6k–8k) prep work (KV cache warmup and attention compute) dominates. Non-streaming 95p latency for a 8k-in/256-out run can be ~200–300ms on an A100-style GPU with q8 quantization if batch size = 1. Streaming reduces time-to-first-byte to ~70–120ms (first token), but total time to finish generating 256 tokens is still in the 250–400ms range depending on model variant and compute.

2) Concurrency and throughput guidance
- To sustain 120 req/s with peaks to 350 concurrency, plan for autoscaling pools and horizontal scaling across machines rather than very large batch sizes — continuous batching + small per-GPU concurrency works best.
- Prefix/KV caching helps a lot for repeated document reads; if 40–60% of requests reuse prefixes we can cut average token compute substantially.

3) Quantization/model variant tradeoffs
- q4_0 / q4_k variants give the best cost/latency tradeoff but require careful validation for quality-sensitive outputs.
- If TTFB is king for interactive UIs, prefer streaming + a slightly smaller decoder model variant for the bulk of traffic; route long-context requests to higher-memory instances with larger context models.

4) Actions we can take now
- We'll run a synthetic testbed with your sample payloads and two model/quantization configs (q4_k streaming on 80GB GPU, and q8 non-streaming on 80GB) and report 50/95/99p TTFB and end-to-response latencies. Expect results within 48 hours.
- I'll include recommended autoscale settings and initial admission control (max inflight per worker) for your pilot.

Attaching preliminary perf export (perf-matrix-0626.csv). Happy to hop on a short call to walk the numbers.
